newsitem.title: USA: U.S. foreign policy figures oppose expanding NATO.
newsitem.headline: U.S. foreign policy figures oppose expanding NATO.

text.p: Pillars of the U.S. foreign policy establishment said on Thursday U.S.-led plans to expand NATO were an "error of historic proportions."

In an open letter to President Bill Clinton, about 50 former U.S. senators, Cabinet secretaries, ambassadors, CIA directors and others called for a postponement of NATO expansion while other European security options were explored.
They said expanding NATO now would play into the hands of the nondemocratic opposition in Russia and undercut proponents of reform and cooperation with the West.
"We ... believe the current U.S.-led effort to expand NATO ... is a policy error of historic proportions," they said.

In Europe, NATO expansion would draw a new line of division between those admitted and those left out that could "foster instability, and ultimately diminish the security of those countries which are not included," the letter said.

The United States, which has spearheaded the diplomatic push to take new democracies into the Atlantic alliance, announced last month it wanted to limit the first intake to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
France and several other members of the alliance want Romania and Slovenia admitted at the same time.
The 16 NATO states are struggling to agree whom they will invite in at a special summit in Madrid on July 8 and 9 that is intended to inaugurate the post-Cold War European security order.
"Russia does not now pose a threat to its western neighbours and the nations of Central and Eastern Europe are not in danger," the U.S. foreign policy leaders wrote.

Among them were Sam Nunn, a Georgia Democrat who retired last year as one of the Senate's foremost defence experts; Ambassador Paul Nitze, President Ronald Reagan's chief arms control negotiator; and Adm. Stansfield Turner, President Jimmy Carter's CIA director.

Signatories also included Jack Matlock, ambassador to the Soviet Union from 1987 to 1991; William Maynes, former editor of Foreign Policy magazine; Philip Merrill, a former NATO assistant secretary-general; and Robert McNamara, secretary of defence from 1961 to 1968 and World Bank president from 1968 to 1991.
